title: The Liquidation of Water: AI, Capital, and the Evaporation of Meaning
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
An essay by Lee Sharks connecting the water demands of AI infrastructure with the Semantic Economy concept of **semantic liquidation**. It argues that data centers can convert water from an ecological and communal relation into a cheap cooling input, while AI composition systems convert situated utterances into decontextualized and fungible retrieval units.

The essay surveys source-reported estimates of water consumption, data-center siting in stressed regions, and alternatives including closed-loop cooling, immersion cooling, wastewater use, waste-heat recovery, location optimization, and compute-efficiency standards. It attributes the persistence of more extractive arrangements to capital allocation, short-term return, and failures of public coordination. The environmental figures and claims of technical availability are dated assertions of the essay and were not independently validated in this description/wiki pass.

modifications.was: The word liquidate comes from the Latin liquidus—to make liquid, to make clear, to dissolve. In finance, it means to convert assets into cash. In violence, it means to eliminate. In both cases, something with structure, relationships, and situated meaning is converted into something fungible, transferable, gone.
